hints: Start by thinking about what type of molecule each column is - an energy carrier, a polysaccharide, a protein, a lipid - and where in a cell you would expect to find it.
Next recall which elements each molecule is built from - which one has three phosphates, which one is only C, H and O, which one has a haem group, which one has a phosphate head.
Now think about plants specifically - which molecules are needed by every living cell for membranes and respiration, and which are unique to plant walls or animal blood.
Finally decide on structural role - ask yourself does this molecule build a lasting structure like a wall or membrane, or is it used for energy transfer or transport.
walkthrough:
Sort Out Phosphorus**
ATP is adenosine triphosphate so it definitely contains P. Phospholipids have a phosphate group in the hydrophilic head, so tick. Cellulose is a polysaccharide of glucose made only of C, H and O, so cross. Haemoglobin is protein plus haem, no P, so cross as given.

Decide Found In Plants**
ATP is made in respiration and photosynthesis in all living cells, so plants have it. Cellulose makes plant cell walls, so plants have it. Phospholipids make all cell surface and organelle membranes, so plants have them. Haemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying pigment in red blood cells of animals, so not in plants.

Sort Out Iron**
Only haemoglobin contains Fe2+ in each haem group to bind oxygen. ATP, cellulose and phospholipid contain no iron, so all cross.

Decide Structural Role**
Cellulose has a strong fibrous wall role and phospholipid forms the structural bilayer of membranes, so both tick. ATP is a soluble energy carrier and haemoglobin is a soluble transport protein, neither builds a structure, so both cross.

Final answer: contains phosphorus: cellulose X, phospholipid tick; found in plants: ATP tick, cellulose tick, haemoglobin X, phospholipid tick; contains iron: ATP X, cellulose X, haemoglobin tick; has a structural role: ATP X, cellulose tick, haemoglobin X, phospholipid tick.

hints: Look carefully at the two ends that will join - the right-hand end of the left amino acid and the left-hand end of the right amino acid. What functional groups are they?
Remember how most biological polymers join - a small molecule is removed when two groups link. Which atoms are lost from COOH and NH2?
Now draw the joined product with the new C-N link in the middle and show the small molecule released, keeping the R groups H and CH3 unchanged.
walkthrough:
Identify The Joining Groups**
You have glycine on the left with R = H and alanine on the right with R = $CH_{3}$. Joining always happens C to N: the carbon of the carboxyl group $-COOH$ on the left links to the nitrogen of the amino group $-NH_{2}$ on the right.

Remove Water By Condensation**
Take $-OH$ off the left $-COOH$ leaving $C=O$, and take $-H$ off the right $-NH_{2}$ leaving $-NH-$. Those combine to form $H_{2}O$. This is why it is called a condensation reaction.

Draw The Dipeptide Correctly**
Draw $H_{2}N-CH_{2}-CO-NH-CH(CH_{3})-COOH$ with a single bond between C and N in the centre. That central $-CO-NH-$ is the peptide bond. Keep all other atoms the same and write $H_{2}O$ as a product.

Final answer: Remove OH from COOH of left amino acid (glycine) and H from NH2 of right amino acid (alanine) to form C-N peptide bond: $H_{2}N-CH_{2}-CO-NH-CH(CH_{3})-COOH + H_{2}O$. Water is released by condensation.

hints: Remember what a glycoprotein is - a protein with a carbohydrate chain sticking out of the cell surface. What could that sugary label be used for by other cells?
Think beyond transport - how do cells stick together, recognise self from non-self, receive hormones, or hold water around the membrane.
walkthrough:
Use The Carbohydrate As A Label**
The branched carbohydrate part projects into the tissue fluid and acts like an ID tag. That lets cells recognise each other, lets the immune system recognise self antigens, and lets cells adhere to each other in tissues.

Use The Protein As A Functional Site**
The protein part can act as a receptor that binds a specific signalling molecule such as a hormone, or act as an enzyme. The carbohydrate can also form hydrogen bonds with water to help stabilise the membrane. Any two of these roles other than transport gain credit.
Final answer: 1. receptor for signalling / binding hormones or neurotransmitters; 2. cell recognition / antigen to allow immune recognition or cell adhesion holding cells together.
